title: Identifying Entities and Relationships
summary: Turning requirements text into a first-pass class model with noun/verb extraction, and deciding is-a versus has-a for every relationship you find.

slides.markdown:
Once requirements are scoped, the next step is turning that text into a first-pass class model — the skeleton the rest of the interview builds on. Two simple techniques do most of the work: pull out the nouns as candidate classes, and the verbs as candidate methods.

This topic covers noun and verb extraction, deciding is-a versus has-a for each relationship, and the two failure modes — modeling everything, and modeling too little.

slides.sectionTitle: Noun extraction: turning requirements into candidate classes
slides.markdown:
Read your written requirements list and underline every noun: vehicle, spot, ticket, gate, lot. Each is a **candidate class** — not a confirmed one, since some nouns turn out to be attributes rather than classes.

For a parking lot: `Vehicle`, `ParkingSpot`, `Ticket`, `ParkingLot`, and `Level` all show up as nouns and all earn a class, because each has its own state and behavior worth tracking independently. A noun like "license plate" also appears, but it's a string attribute on `Vehicle`, not a class of its own.

Noun extraction is fast and mechanical — the judgment call is deciding which nouns actually deserve a class.

slides.sectionTitle: Verb extraction: turning requirements into candidate methods and behaviors
slides.markdown:
Now underline the verbs: park, unpark, calculate fee, assign spot, issue ticket. Each verb becomes a **candidate method**, and which noun it attaches to is often the interesting design decision.

"Calculate fee" could live on `Ticket` (it knows entry and exit time), on `ParkingLot` (it knows the pricing rules), or on a separate fee-calculator class — the verb alone doesn't decide, the requirements do. If pricing varies by vehicle type and might change independently of the lot, that's a hint toward a separate strategy-like class rather than bolting it onto `Ticket`.

Verb extraction gives you the method list; deciding ownership is where the actual design skill shows.

slides.sectionTitle: Deciding is-a vs has-a for each relationship found
slides.markdown:
For every relationship between two candidate classes, ask: is this **is-a** (inheritance — a `Car` is a `Vehicle`) or **has-a** (composition — a `ParkingLot` has `Level`s, a `Level` has `ParkingSpot`s)?

Getting this wrong is a common LLD misstep: modeling `Motorcycle` and `Car` as unrelated classes duplicates shared behavior, while modeling `ParkingSpot` as a subclass of `Vehicle` confuses containment with type. A tiebreaker helps: if you can say "a _ is a kind of _", it's is-a; if you say "a _ has a _" or "a _ contains _", it's has-a.

Most real designs lean has-a more than beginners expect — composition tends to age better than deep inheritance trees, since it's easier to change what a class contains than what it inherits from.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: entities and relationships sketched from a sample prompt
slides.markdown:
![Parking lot entities: has-a backbone from lot to level to spot, is-a for vehicle types, Ticket ties both together](assets/parking-lot-entities.svg)

Notice the shape: containment (has-a) forms the backbone — lot contains levels contains spots — while inheritance (is-a) is used sparingly, only where vehicle types genuinely share behavior. `Ticket` ties the two structures together by referencing both a vehicle and a spot.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a first-pass class skeleton generated from a requirements list
Pitfall: modeling every noun as a class, including ones that are just attributes
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Every noun in the requirements deserves its own class — license plate, timestamp, fee amount, all of it."

**Why it's wrong:** most nouns are attributes, not entities. A license plate has no independent behavior or lifecycle — it's a string that belongs to `Vehicle`. Turning it into a class adds indirection without adding meaning, and an interviewer watching you create a `LicensePlate` class for a plain string will read it as not knowing where to draw the line.

**Correct model:** a noun earns a class when it has its own state **and** behavior, or a lifecycle independent of its container — `Ticket` qualifies (it's created, closed, and calculates its own fee); "entry timestamp" doesn't.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: a too-flat model vs a too-fragmented one
slides.markdown:
| | Too-flat model | Too-fragmented model |
|---|---|---|
| Symptom | One `ParkingLot` class with 15+ methods and fields | A class for every noun, including plain attributes |
| Why it happens | Avoiding the effort of splitting responsibilities | Over-applying "every noun is a class" |
| What breaks | A single change (new pricing rule) touches unrelated code | Simple operations require chasing five objects |
| Fix | Split by responsibility: pricing, spot assignment, ticketing | Merge classes that have no independent state or behavior |

**How to decide:** a class is right-sized if you can describe its job in one sentence without using "and," and if merging it into its neighbor wouldn't lose any independently-changing behavior.
